characters: Yaw: an eleven-year-old Ghanaian boy in Primary 6, observant and caring, wearing a sky-blue polo shirt and khaki shorts, carrying a bright yellow umbrella.
Auntie Akosua: Yaw’s mother, a wise seamstress in her thirties, wearing a neat blue-and-yellow wax-print dress.
Uncle Tetteh: a friendly neighbourhood provision shopkeeper in his forties, wearing a brown collared shirt.
Mrs Mensah: a licensed insurance officer in her thirties, wearing a smart navy jacket and carrying an inspection clipboard.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, expressive Ghanaian storyteller (en-GH); wise and steady for Auntie Akosua and Mrs Mensah.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 115 words per minute); clear pauses for the risk-pooling and deductible arithmetic.

music: Optional gentle rain sound effect on page 2 giving way to bright acoustic guitar; off by default.
culturalNotes: Connects insurance literacy to Ghana’s familiar National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and the National Insurance Commission (NIC).
reviewQuestions: Are the concepts of risk pooling, deductibles and exclusions clear for Primary 5–JHS 1 learners?

pages.brief: Lively Ghanaian neighbourhood street as dark blue storm clouds gather: Yaw (11, sky-blue polo shirt, khaki shorts) holding a closed yellow umbrella outside Auntie Akosua’s tailoring shop while Uncle Tetteh waves cheerfully from the shop next door.
pages.narration: Warm, memorable opening metaphor: you prepare the umbrella before the rain begins.

pages.brief: Morning light after a storm: a large broken tree branch resting across the corner roofs of two neighbouring shops; puddles on the ground as Yaw, Auntie Akosua and Uncle Tetteh inspect the damage with concern.
pages.narration: Dramatic storm night followed by sympathetic morning discovery.

pages.brief: Outside the two shops: Uncle Tetteh sitting sadly on a crate beside damp cardboard boxes, while Auntie Akosua holds a clean official document folder from a waterproof tin as Yaw watches closely.
pages.narration: Contrast Uncle Tetteh’s distress with Auntie Akosua’s calm preparation.

pages.brief: Auntie Akosua sitting with Yaw and Uncle Tetteh on a dry bench, sketching a visual diagram of many small hands placing coins into a giant central pot under a big yellow umbrella (no text or numbers).
pages.narration: Clear, step-by-step arithmetic of risk pooling: 100 shopkeepers × 100 cedis = 10,000 cedis in the shared pool.

pages.brief: Close view of the visual diagram: golden coins flowing from the central umbrella pot to repair two little shop roofs, while rows of other little shops stand safe in the sunshine (no text).
pages.narration: Make the logic of risk pooling click clearly for upper-primary and JHS listeners.

pages.brief: Outside Auntie Akosua’s shop: Mrs Mensah (navy jacket, clipboard) photographing the broken roof eave while Auntie Akosua and Yaw stand beside a local carpenter holding a wooden measuring rule.
pages.narration: Professional, reassuring process of filing and verifying an honest claim.

pages.brief: At Auntie Akosua’s worktable: Mrs Mensah placing two small coin stacks on one side and eighteen coin stacks on the other side to show how the repair bill is shared (no text).
pages.narration: Walk clearly through the deductible maths: 2,000 repair minus 200 deductible equals 1,800 payout.

pages.brief: Mrs Mensah holding up an official certificate card with a gold shield emblem (no text) while Yaw and Uncle Tetteh listen attentively.
pages.narration: Important consumer education: policy conditions, exclusions (wear and tear vs sudden loss), honesty, and NIC Ghana regulation.

pages.brief: Inside the tailoring shop, already being repaired by the carpenter in the background: Yaw holding up a blue-and-gold health card (no text) with a bright smile as Auntie Akosua and Mrs Mensah nod.
pages.narration: Connect property insurance to everyday Ghanaian life through the NHIS and emergency savings.

pages.brief: Sunny neighbourhood street outside both newly repaired shops: Uncle Tetteh holding a new policy folder and smiling warmly at Yaw and Auntie Akosua.

teacherGuide.overview: An upper-primary and JHS 1 financial literacy story that uses the vivid metaphor of "buying an umbrella before the rain" to explain risk pooling, premiums, claims, deductibles, policy conditions/exclusions, Ghana’s National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS), regulation by the National Insurance Commission (NIC), and why families need both emergency savings and insurance.
learningGoals: Explain how risk pooling spreads the cost of rare, expensive disasters across many contributors (100 × 100 = 10,000 cedis pool).
Define premium, policy, claim, deductible and exclusions accurately.
Calculate an insurance payout after subtracting a deductible (2,000 − 200 = 1,800 cedis).
Identify the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) and the National Insurance Commission (NIC) in Ghana.
beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Classroom Risk-Pool Game: 20 pupils each place 1 paper token into a "Class Pencil-Replacement Pool". Draw 2 random names of pupils who suffered a "sudden broken ruler/pencil storm" and award 5 tokens each from the pool to replace their tools.
Deductible Maths Practice: Solve three repair problems with different deductibles (e.g., 1,500-cedi repair with a 150-cedi deductible → 1,350-cedi payout).
discussion: Why did Auntie Akosua say "once the storm is pouring, it is too late to go shopping for an umbrella"?
How can an insurance company afford to pay 1,800 cedis to repair Auntie Akosua’s roof when her annual premium was much smaller?
Why does an insurance policy cover a sudden storm branch falling on a roof, but NOT a roof that slowly rusted over fifteen years without maintenance?
Why did Auntie Akosua still need a small emergency savings fund even though she had shop insurance?
reflection: Why did Auntie Akosua still need a small emergency savings fund even though she had shop insurance?

whatWeKnow: Risk pooling relies on the Law of Large Numbers: while an individual cannot predict whether a storm will hit their shop this year, a large pool of policyholders experiences a predictable average rate of losses.
In Ghana, the National Insurance Commission (NIC) regulates insurance companies and intermediaries, and the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) pools health risks across the population.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Actuaries and agricultural scientists in Ghana are developing satellite-based weather-index micro-insurance to help smallholder farmers recover from severe droughts or floods.

investigation.title: Risk-Pooling Dice Simulation
materials: Six groups of pupils, one 6-sided die, and 60 counters (10 counters per group).
steps: Round 1 (No Insurance Pool): Each group keeps its 10 counters. Roll the die, whichever group number is rolled suffers a "storm loss" of 12 counters (more than they have!).
Round 2 (Risk Pool): Each of the 6 groups contributes 3 counters (premium) into a central Umbrella Pool (6 × 3 = 18 counters in the pool, leaving 7 counters per group).
Roll the die for the storm loss of 12 counters: the Umbrella Pool pays 11 counters and the affected group pays a 1-counter deductible, every group stays afloat!
